posts.title: OpenAI is already trying to shape the 2028 election | TechCrunch
posts.author: Rebecca Bellan
posts.summary: OpenAI’s chief global affairs officer Chris Lehane has released an essay likening AI’s potential to reshape the economy to Franklin D. Roosevelt’s New Deal, outlining five policy priorities that include worker protections, education, AI safety, and data‑center development. The piece marks a shift from OpenAI’s previous focus on accelerating AI and reducing regulatory barriers, and it urges politicians to create a “compelling third path” that lets ordinary Americans share in AI’s benefits. Critics from the AI Now Institute argue that Lehane’s proposals still favor the company, lack concrete measures to prevent wealth concentration, and rely on unproven assumptions about AI’s positive impact on learning and jobs. The essay arrives amid a post‑midterm political climate where data‑center opposition and affordability concerns are rising, positioning AI as a likely central issue in the 2028 election.
key_points: OpenAI’s Chris Lehane proposes a New Deal‑style policy agenda for AI, emphasizing worker protections, education, safety, and data‑center expansion.
The essay signals a shift from OpenAI’s earlier push for fewer regulations to a more policy‑oriented stance, but critics say it still favors the company.
Critics argue the proposals lack concrete measures to prevent wealth concentration and question the feasibility of AI‑driven prosperity.

posts.title: Food delivery startup Wonder files for IPO as it explores its next big bite | TechCrunch
posts.author: Lauren Forristal
posts.summary: Food delivery startup Wonder has confidentially filed for an IPO, marking a significant step toward becoming a public company after years of fundraising and expansion. Founded in 2018 by Marc Lore, the company has shifted from a delivery app to a food‑technology platform that operates food‑hall style locations, handles meal prep, and offers dine‑in service. Wonder recently raised over $650 million in a round that valued it at roughly $9 billion, and it plans aggressive growth, including more than 100 new Texas locations by 2027. The IPO will bring new scrutiny as Wonder competes with established players like DoorDash and Uber Eats while leveraging acquisitions such as Blue Apron, Grubhub, Tastemade, and Spyce.
key_points: Wonder has filed confidentially for an IPO after raising $650M at a $9B valuation.
The company operates food‑hall style locations and handles end‑to‑end meal prep, delivery, pickup, and dine‑in.
It plans to open over 100 new Texas locations by 2027 and has acquired Blue Apron, Grubhub, Tastemade, and Spyce.
The IPO will subject Wonder to increased competition from DoorDash, Uber Eats, and other delivery giants.

posts.title: Bluesky hit peak usage for the year on election night | TechCrunch
posts.author: Amanda Silberling
posts.summary: Bluesky recorded its highest daily activity on U.S. midterm election night, with 44 million likes, 4.8 million posts, and 2 million new follows on November 4, 2026. The platform’s traffic spiked to 35.8 GB/s, a 200 % increase over normal levels, while likes rose 70 % and posts 30 % above the 30‑day average. CEO Toni Schneider noted a surge of new users and returning members, and COO Rose Wang said peak engagement occurred between 8 p.m. and 10 p.m. PT as election results unfolded. The spike reflects Bluesky’s left‑leaning user base, which grew after Donald Trump’s 2024 loss and is now highly active during Democratic victories.
key_points: Bluesky hit 44 million likes on election night, close to its all‑time record of 45 million.
Daily posts and likes jumped 30 % and 70 % over the 30‑day average.
Traffic surged to 35.8 GB/s, a 200 % increase from typical levels.

posts.title: TikTok quietly launches a stand-alone TikTok Shop app | TechCrunch
posts.author: Aisha Malik
posts.summary: TikTok has quietly launched a dedicated TikTok Shop app in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, and the Philippines, offering personalized product recommendations, livestream and short‑form video shopping, app‑exclusive deals, in‑app checkout, order tracking, and customer support. The move gives TikTok a separate storefront to reach shoppers beyond its main platform and to compete more directly with e‑commerce giants such as Amazon, Temu, Walmart, and Target. While the company has not confirmed a U.S. rollout, the app’s launch signals a deeper investment in social commerce and a broader strategy that includes games, restaurant guides, sports hubs, hotel booking, and payments. TikTok’s new app also mirrors Amazon’s earlier attempt to lure users away from TikTok with its Inspire feed, creating a full‑circle rivalry in the e‑commerce space.
key_points: TikTok launched a stand‑alone TikTok Shop app in four Southeast Asian markets with features like livestream shopping and app‑exclusive deals
The app positions TikTok to compete directly with Amazon, Temu, Walmart, and Target by offering a dedicated shopping destination
TikTok’s broader strategy includes expanding into games, travel, and payments, indicating a shift beyond social media

posts.title: Dropbox acquires Tigris Data for $350M to bolster its AI infrastructure | TechCrunch
posts.author: Lauren Forristal
posts.summary: Dropbox announced a $350 million acquisition of cloud‑storage firm Tigris Data to strengthen its AI infrastructure and launch DBX Agent Cloud, a new storage platform for businesses and developers building AI models and agents. The deal, expected to close in the fourth quarter of 2026, will not involve headcount reductions and will allow customers to purchase object storage that is compatible with Amazon S3 and other existing tools. Dropbox plans to expand DBX Agent Cloud with support for documents, images, audio, and video, and to add filesystem features that let AI agents manage files across tasks and sessions. The acquisition follows Dropbox’s prior AI‑focused purchases and positions the company to offer more AI capabilities in its core product, including integration with ChatGPT, Claude, and Muse.
key_points: Dropbox acquires Tigris Data for $350M to expand AI infrastructure
Deal to close Q4 2026 with no headcount cuts
DBX Agent Cloud will provide standalone object storage compatible with Amazon S3
Tigris Data, founded by former Uber engineers, raised $25M Series A last year

posts.title: AI PACs spent millions trying to shape Congress — here's how they fared | TechCrunch
posts.author: Rebecca Bellan
posts.summary: AI‑focused political action committees poured millions into the 2024 midterm elections, but the results were uneven: heavily backed candidates such as South Carolina Senate hopeful Darline Graham lost despite $4.8 million from American Mission and Building the Future.  Leading the Future’s primary‑focused strategy saw $27.38 million spent on name‑recognition efforts, while Guardrails Alliance spent over $1 million opposing candidates it deemed too close to AI money.  The mixed outcomes mirror the broader Democratic wave, yet both sides—LTF’s push for a national AI framework and Guardrails Alliance’s campaign to make AI funding politically toxic—plan to keep investing in the 2028 cycle.  The race underscores the ongoing debate over whether Congress should adopt a single federal AI policy or allow states to set their own safeguards.
key_points: AI PACs spent $4.8 million on SC Senate candidate Darline Graham, who lost;
Leading the Future invested $27.38 million in primaries to build name recognition;
Guardrails Alliance spent >$1 million opposing candidates to make AI money toxic;
Mixed results reflect the broader Democratic wave in the 2024 midterms

posts.title: Harbinger raises $240M after expanding into defense | TechCrunch
posts.author: Sean O'Kane
posts.summary: Harbinger, the Los Angeles‑based electric truck startup, closed a $240 million Series D round, bringing its total funding to over $650 million. The round was co‑led by Tiger Global, Capricorn’s technology impact fund, and defense‑focused Ridgeline, with repeat investors FedEx, Maniv, Greycroft, Leitmotif and Fidelity Management. FedEx deepened its partnership by adding senior VP Paul Melander to Harbinger’s board and placing a first large order for 2,000 trucks worth more than $300 million. Founded in 2022 by former Canoo and QuantumScape employees, Harbinger has broadened its product line to include battery storage, hybrid emergency vehicles, a driverless hybrid electric platform for the military, and the acquisition of autonomy startup Phantom AI.
key_points: Harbinger raised $240 million in a Series D, co‑led by Tiger Global, Capricorn, and Ridgeline, after a $160 million Series C the previous year.
FedEx invested again, joined the board, and placed a $300 million order for 2,000 trucks.
The company has expanded beyond a single truck chassis to battery storage, hybrid emergency vehicles, a driverless military platform, and the acquisition of Phantom AI.
Harbinger’s total capital exceeds $650 million and it is reportedly considering an IPO.

posts.title: Axiom Math wants to keep AI slop out of mathematics | TechCrunch
posts.author: Aditya Mehta
posts.summary: Axiom Math announced that it has formally verified the Stacks Project, a massive open‑source mathematics library, by translating its 7,654 pages into about 16 million lines of Lean code that a proof assistant checks line by line. The verification provides a reliable, logically sound foundation that AI agents can use to write software and conduct scientific research, potentially preventing the “AI slop” that has plagued recent automated math claims. The startup, founded by 25‑year‑old CEO Carina Hong, raised a $200 million Series A led by Menlo Ventures in March 2025 to support this effort. By training its own models to understand mathematical taste, Axiom aims to make verified math a reusable library for both mathematicians and developers, encouraging the broader industry to adopt formal verification at scale.
key_points: Axiom Math has formally verified the Stacks Project, producing 16 million lines of Lean code that passes proof‑assistant checks.
The verified library serves as a reliable foundation for AI agents to write software and conduct scientific work, reducing the risk of AI-generated errors.
The company secured a $200 million Series A round led by Menlo Ventures to fund its formal‑verification platform.
CEO Carina Hong stresses the importance of a reusable, verified mathematical base to prevent AI slop and invites other firms to scale formalization efforts.

posts.title: Amazon ditches Grubhub, taps Uber Eats for Prime | TechCrunch
posts.author: Kirsten Korosec
posts.summary: Amazon has replaced its restaurant delivery partnership with Grubhub with Uber Eats for Prime members in the United States, ending a multi‑year agreement that began in 2022. Prime customers can now order food through Amazon.com or the Shopping app without creating an Uber account and receive free delivery on orders over $25, with a $20 discount on the first two qualifying orders. The switch follows Amazon’s evaluation of third‑party offers and its desire to provide a better delivery experience, while existing Grubhub+ members retain access until December 31 2027. The move deepens Amazon’s broader collaboration with Uber, which already spans cloud services, autonomous vehicles, and Alexa integration.
key_points: Amazon ends its 2022‑started partnership with Grubhub and replaces it with Uber Eats for Prime members.
Prime members can order through Amazon without an Uber account and get free delivery on orders over $25, plus a $20 discount on the first two orders.
Grubhub+ subscribers keep their membership through Dec 31 2027, but new orders via Amazon will no longer use Grubhub.
The change expands Amazon’s existing ties to Uber, covering cloud, autonomous vehicles, and Alexa integration.

posts.title: 'You Can See Everything' is getting an outer space release and it hasn't even come out in Europe yet | TechCrunch
posts.author: Amanda Silberling
posts.summary: A24, the studio behind the Elizabeth Holmes documentary "You Can See Everything," has granted NASA a request to screen the film on the International Space Station, making it available to astronauts before it even hits European theaters. The film, which debuted in North America with a limited theatrical rollout, has topped the box‑office charts and is generating demand worldwide. Sony Pictures has secured theatrical rights for Germany, Latin America, South Korea, and other territories, while the UK release is slated for November 20 and France for December 30. This unique outer‑space premiere underscores the film’s global buzz and the growing interest in the Holmes saga.
key_points: A24 approved a NASA request to screen "You Can See Everything" on the ISS before its European release
The film has topped the box office and is generating worldwide demand
Sony Pictures holds theatrical rights for Germany, Latin America, South Korea, and other territories
UK and French releases are scheduled for November 20 and December 30, respectively

posts.title: Founder Summit 2026: Doors open at 9 a.m. ET in Boston | TechCrunch
posts.author: TechCrunch Events
posts.summary: TechCrunch’s Founder Summit 2026 opened its doors at 9 a.m. ET in Boston’s SoWa Power Station, marking the end of discounted pricing and the start of full‑rate tickets. The full day features keynote panels, interactive roundtables, and breakout sessions covering fundraising, product‑market fit, AI innovation, and enterprise growth, with speakers such as Steve Fredette of Toast and Amulya Vishwanath of Techable Ventures. Attendees can network through the Expo Hall and a Braindate‑powered lounge, scheduling one‑on‑one meetings with founders, investors, and operators. Early registrants still have a chance to save up to $100 on a pass and receive a second pass for free before the BOGO offer expires.
key_points: Doors opened at 9 a.m. ET, ending discounted pricing for the Founder Summit 2026 in Boston
Early registration offers up to $100 savings and a buy‑one‑get‑one‑free pass
The event includes keynote panels, breakout sessions, and roundtables on fundraising, AI, and product‑market fit
Networking is facilitated via the Expo Hall and a Braindate‑powered lounge

posts.title: US government warns of 'ongoing cyber threat' amid mass hacks of industrial retail and military freezers | TechCrunch
posts.author: Zack Whittaker
posts.summary: The U.S. government has issued a joint warning that an "ongoing cyber threat" is targeting industrial refrigeration units in grocery stores, cold storage facilities, military bases, and even a blood bank.  Recent attacks across the United Kingdom, Europe, and the United States have forced freezers to raise temperatures, risking food spoilage, fire hazards, and inventory loss.  While no group has been officially named, security researchers and U.S. officials point to Iran as the likely culprit.  Federal agencies urge affected operators to disconnect remote‑control systems from the internet, strengthen passwords, apply patches, and retire unsupported equipment to mitigate the risk.
key_points: U.S. agencies warn of an ongoing cyber threat to industrial refrigeration units worldwide
Attacks have caused temperature changes that can lead to food spoilage, fire hazards, and inventory loss
Security researchers attribute the attacks to Iran, affecting grocery stores, military bases, and a blood bank
Affected operators are advised to disconnect remote control, patch systems, strengthen passwords, and retire unsupported equipment

posts.title: OpenAI president Greg Brockman says company could be IPO ready in 2027 | TechCrunch
posts.author: Sarah Perez
posts.summary: OpenAI president Greg Brockman announced that the company could be ready for an IPO in 2027, citing strong enterprise revenue growth and a shift from a consumer‑focused model to a business‑centric strategy. He highlighted a 70% quarterly growth in annualized revenue during Q3 2026, driven largely by the enterprise segment now accounting for roughly 70% of total revenue. Brockman noted key wins such as a partnership with JPMorgan Chase and emphasized the company’s confidence in its long‑term business model. The announcement underscores OpenAI’s ambition to go public when market conditions and internal readiness align.
key_points: OpenAI aims for an IPO in 2027
Enterprise revenue grew 70% in Q3 2026 and now makes up about 70% of total revenue
The company has pivoted from a consumer focus to winning large enterprise clients like JPMorgan Chase
Brockman expressed strong confidence in OpenAI’s business trajectory and readiness for public markets

posts.title: Apple is reportedly cutting budgets for its internal AI usage | TechCrunch
posts.author: Lucas Ropek
posts.summary: Apple has announced a reduction in the daily AI spending limits for its engineering teams, cutting the cap from $300 to $200 and potentially down to $100 for some groups, while non‑engineering departments may face limits as low as $25. The move follows a broader industry trend of token rationing after a wave of tokenmaxxing that drove up costs. Apple’s decision signals a shift toward tighter fiscal discipline as the company weighs the real productivity gains of AI against its expense. The change underscores growing uncertainty about the cost‑benefit balance of AI adoption in large tech firms.
key_points: Apple cuts daily AI spending caps for engineering teams from $300 to $200, with some groups potentially limited to $100.
Non‑engineering departments may face limits as low as $25 per day.
The move reflects a broader industry shift toward token rationing after high‑cost tokenmaxxing.
Apple’s decision highlights uncertainty about AI’s productivity gains versus its costs.

posts.title: After the midterms, a bigger clash over data centers could be coming | TechCrunch
posts.author: Dominic-Madori Davis
posts.summary: The November 3 midterm election gave Democrats full control of Congress, setting the stage for a potential clash over data centers that power AI. Voters in several states, especially Ohio and Texas, pushed back against large AI buildouts, with local bans and opposition to projects like OpenAI’s $500 billion center and Meta’s 700,000‑sq‑ft facility. Democratic lawmakers now face the possibility of nationwide moratoriums or stricter guardrails, including bills introduced by Sanders and Ocasio‑Cortez and the GRID Savings Act, to curb environmental impacts and protect community interests. The backlash reflects broader concerns that AI infrastructure may enrich a few while burdening local residents with power costs and environmental harm.
key_points: Democratic control of Congress could enable nationwide data‑center moratoriums and stricter regulations
Voter opposition in states such as Ohio and Texas has led to local bans and heightened scrutiny of AI buildouts
Legislative proposals like the Sanders/Ocasio‑Cortez bill and the GRID Savings Act aim to curb environmental and community costs
The debate underscores fears that AI infrastructure may disproportionately benefit corporations while harming local communities

posts.title: Open source AI is booming. Hugging Face explains who profits. | TechCrunch
posts.author: Theresa Loconsolo
posts.summary: Open‑source AI models are moving from niche to mainstream, with enterprises, governments and startups citing lower costs, greater control and flexibility as key drivers. Yet as these models become more powerful and freely available, companies face the challenge of capturing value and navigating trade‑offs in tooling, infrastructure and policy. In a recent Equity podcast, Hugging Face’s Irene Solaiman explained how startups can choose the right open‑source tools and strategies to stay competitive, especially amid growing Chinese open‑model offerings. The discussion highlights the growing importance of open‑source AI ecosystems and the need for clear value‑capture frameworks.
key_points: Open‑source AI models are increasingly mainstream, offering lower costs and greater control.
Companies must navigate tool selection, infrastructure, and policy trade‑offs to capture value from open models.
Chinese open‑model offerings are gaining traction, challenging U.S. players.
Hugging Face’s Irene Solaiman outlines strategies for startups building on open models.

posts.title: DuckDuckGo pitches itself to schools amid backlash over Google's AI policy | TechCrunch
posts.author: Sarah Perez
posts.summary: DuckDuckGo is positioning itself as a privacy‑focused alternative for schools after Google announced that it would disable Gemini and other AI features by default in K‑12 environments, a move that sparked backlash from educators who want more control over AI in classrooms. The search engine’s CEO and public affairs officer publicly criticized Google’s decision, urging schools to switch to DuckDuckGo’s default search engine and highlighting the company’s ability to turn off AI features entirely. DuckDuckGo’s own AI offerings, such as Duck.ai, can be disabled, and the company reported a 30% rise in app installs earlier this year as users rejected forced AI from Google Search. By providing clear documentation and support for switching, DuckDuckGo aims to capture a share of the 50 million Chromebooks in schools and the 150 million users of Google Classroom worldwide.
key_points: Google will disable Gemini and other AI features by default in K‑12 schools, prompting DuckDuckGo to pitch itself as a privacy‑focused alternative
DuckDuckGo’s leadership publicly criticized Google’s AI enforcement and offered schools a way to switch the default search engine
DuckDuckGo’s AI features can be turned off, and the company saw a 30% increase in app installs after users rejected forced AI from Google Search
DuckDuckGo provides documentation and support for schools to change their default search engine to its service

posts.title: Waymo confirms it's shaking up its Uber relationship in January 2028 | TechCrunch
posts.author: Sean O'Kane
posts.summary: Waymo announced it will end its exclusivity agreement with Uber in the Austin and Atlanta markets beginning January 2028, opting to offer robotaxi rides directly through its own smartphone app. Uber confirmed it will continue to host Waymo robotaxis on its platform for as long as the two companies agree. The move follows rider feedback that the partnership made it unclear whether a booking would be a human‑driven or autonomous vehicle, prompting Waymo to seek a more predictable booking experience. Waymo’s co‑CEO Tekedra Mawakana said the decision was driven by the need for a stronger relationship with riders and the desire to provide a consistent service.
key_points: Waymo ends exclusivity with Uber in Austin and Atlanta effective January 2028
Waymo will launch its own app for robotaxi rides in those markets
Uber will continue to host Waymo robotaxis on its app until the agreement ends
Rider experience inconsistencies prompted Waymo to pursue direct booking options

posts.title: I tried Apple's Siri Recaps. They're surprisingly useful — and a little unsettling | TechCrunch
posts.author: Sarah Perez
posts.summary: Apple’s latest iOS 27.3 and watchOS 27.3 developer betas introduce four new audio‑intelligence features, including sound and song detection, Live Rewind, and Siri Recaps. The author tested Siri Recaps on an Apple Watch and found it can automatically capture and summarize spoken details from everyday conversations, which can be handy for remembering fast‑paced information such as repair estimates or family errands. However, the feature also records non‑essential chatter and mixes unrelated topics into a single note, raising privacy concerns about the device always listening. The article ends with suggestions for Apple to allow separate note sections, easier bullet‑point deletion, and automatic export to the Notes app.
key_points: Apple introduced Siri Recaps and Live Rewind in the iOS 27.3/watchOS 27.3 beta
Siri Recaps automatically records and summarizes conversations, useful for capturing fast‑paced details
The feature can capture extraneous information and mix unrelated topics, raising privacy concerns
The author suggests separate note sections, easier deletion, and auto‑export to Notes

posts.title: TechCrunch Mobility: A new, bigger AV boom is here | TechCrunch
posts.author: Kirsten Korosec
posts.summary: TechCrunch Mobility reports a new, larger autonomous‑vehicle wave in 2026, driven by AI foundation models that lower entry barriers and enable rapid startup deployment. Trucks VC has received pitches from 81 AV companies—two‑thirds more than 2025—many targeting robotaxi services that could compete with Waymo in niche markets. The article also highlights significant funding moves, including Re:Build’s $2.1 billion raise, Bedrock Robotics’ $600 million Series C that values it at $4.1 billion, and DoorDash’s $17 billion acquisition of Instacart. These developments underscore a broader shift toward AI‑powered mobility and the growing commercial interest in autonomous technology.
key_points: 2026 sees a second AV wave fueled by AI foundation models
Trucks VC received 81 pitches, two‑thirds more than 2025
Re:Build raised $2.1 billion to scale hard‑tech manufacturing
Bedrock Robotics valued at $4.1 billion after $600 million Series C

posts.title: Snapchat surpasses 30M paid subscribers | TechCrunch
posts.author: Aisha Malik
posts.summary: Snapchat announced it has surpassed 30 million paid subscribers across its Snapchat+, Memories Storage, and Lens+ plans, a jump of five million from the 25 million mark reported in February. The milestone comes after the company introduced higher‑tier options—Lens+ at $8.99/month and Snapchat+ Platinum at $15.99/month—to diversify revenue and capitalize on AI‑powered features. In its third‑quarter 2026 earnings release, Snap reported 495 million daily active users, slightly below analyst expectations, and its shares fell 12% after missing ad‑revenue and user‑growth estimates.
key_points: Snapchat reached 30 million paid subscribers, up from 25 million in February
New subscription tiers Lens+ and Snapchat+ Platinum broaden revenue streams
Earnings miss led to a 12% drop in Snap shares
Daily active users hit 495 million, below the 499 million forecast

posts.title: Meta acquires AI coding startup Conductor | TechCrunch
posts.author: Lucas Ropek
posts.summary: Meta has acquired Conductor, an AI coding startup that lets users spin up software projects by deploying multiple agents into parallel workspaces. Conductor, founded in 2024 and launched its core product last summer, uses agentic teams sourced from major labs such as Anthropic and OpenAI to help engineers work on compartmentalized parts of a project. Meta confirmed the deal but did not disclose terms; Conductor will keep its core features active until early next year while its cloud service will shut down on November 20, after which user cloud data will be deleted. The acquisition underscores Meta’s push to catch up in AI coding tools, following the launch of Muse Code, the adoption of Muse agents, and other AI-related acquisitions like Moltbook.
key_points: Meta acquires Conductor, an AI coding startup that deploys agentic teams into parallel workspaces
Conductor’s cloud service will shut down on November 20, with core features remaining until early next year
Meta is expanding its AI coding ecosystem with Muse Code, Muse agents, and recent acquisitions such as Moltbook
Conductor’s agents are sourced from major labs like Anthropic and OpenAI

posts.title: Hackers stole DreamHost customer files and inboxes during months-long attack | TechCrunch
posts.author: Zack Whittaker
posts.summary: DreamHost confirmed a months‑long cyberattack that compromised customer emails and credentials. The breach, which began in August, exploited an unspecified vulnerability in the company’s file manager, allowing attackers to steal session tokens and log in as users. The incident triggered a multi‑day outage during which DreamHost reset passwords, and the company estimates fewer than 10% of its roughly 400,000 paying customers were affected. DreamHost has filed a data‑breach notice with California’s attorney general and is still investigating why the attack went undetected for weeks.
key_points: DreamHost confirmed a months‑long breach stealing emails and credentials.
The attack began in August, exploiting a file manager vulnerability and stealing session tokens.
The breach caused a multi‑day outage and prompted password resets.
Less than 10% of the 400,000 customers were affected, and the company is investigating detection delays.

posts.title: Revolut's valuation jumps 53% to $115B in new share sale as it prepares to launch US bank | TechCrunch
posts.author: Jagmeet Singh
posts.summary: Revolut’s latest secondary share sale has pushed its valuation to $115 billion, a 53% increase over last year’s price, even though the deal did not bring in new capital. The London‑based fintech, founded in 2015 by Nik Storonsky and Vlad Yatsenko, is now preparing to launch a national U.S. bank in the first half of 2027 after receiving conditional approval from the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency. Business banking, which accounts for about 20% of Revolut’s gross profit, is expanding rapidly—processing roughly $48.6 billion in monthly transactions and targeting 1 million business customers by 2027. The company is also weighing a dual listing in New York and London, with an IPO potentially valued at $200 billion not expected before 2028.
key_points: Revolut’s valuation rose to $115 billion in a secondary share sale that raised no new money
The fintech is set to launch a U.S. bank in 2027 after conditional OCC approval
Business banking now contributes about 20% of gross profit and aims to grow to 1 million customers by 2027
Revolut is considering a dual NY/London IPO that could value it at $200 billion around 2028

posts.title: India's EloElo nabs $80M from NBCUniversal to bet on the country's rising microdrama market | TechCrunch
posts.author: Ivan Mehta
posts.summary: EloElo, the Indian microdrama platform behind Story TV, has closed an $80 million Series C round led by Hornbill Capital and NBCUniversal, bringing its total funding to $130 million and a $500 million valuation. The deal underscores the rapid growth of India’s microdrama market, where 118 million users stream serialized content each month and Story TV alone boasts 33 million active users. EloElo plans to deploy the capital to expand its AI‑powered content creation tools and original programming while scaling its workforce to 240 employees. The investment signals confidence that India’s mobile‑first entertainment sector could generate $3‑$4 billion in annual revenue by 2030.
key_points: EloElo raised $80 million in Series C from Hornbill Capital and NBCUniversal, raising total funding to $130 million and valuing the company at $500 million
India’s microdrama market attracts 118 million monthly viewers and Story TV has 33 million active users
The company will use the new capital to expand its Dolphin AI content‑creation platform and original titles
EloElo’s workforce is 240 people and it serves over 40 million monthly users across its apps

posts.title: Nothing CEO says company's mysterious AI-first device is dropping next month | TechCrunch
posts.author: Lucas Ropek
posts.summary: Nothing’s CEO Carl Pei announced that the company’s first AI‑native product will ship in December. The device is described as a screenless, non‑app productivity tool built with the brand’s characteristic personality and care. Pei also mentioned plans for AI‑linked smart glasses and earbuds, but emphasized that the new product is distinct from wearables. While a firm release date has not been set, the announcement signals Nothing’s push into AI‑first consumer hardware.
key_points: Nothing’s first AI‑native product will ship in December and is a screenless, non‑app productivity tool.
The device is built with Nothing’s characteristic personality and care.
Pei also plans AI‑linked smart glasses and earbuds, but the new product is distinct from wearables.
No firm release date has been announced yet, but the December shipping date is confirmed.

posts.title: Almost no one uses AI agents to book their Uber, company says | TechCrunch
posts.author: Sarah Perez
posts.summary: Uber reported that only four rides were booked through AI agents during its busiest week in October, and just 500 Uber Eats orders were placed by AI agents out of 320 million total trips and orders. The company’s CFO highlighted the limited traction, while CEO Dara Khosrowshahi expressed optimism that AI agents could boost demand across the platform. Despite the hype around personal AI assistants, the average booking time in Uber’s app is already short, so the time savings from agents are minimal. Uber remains bullish on the potential of AI agents, noting that the number of major assistants is growing and that many AI companies are engaging with the company.
key_points: Only four Uber rides were booked via AI agents in the busiest week of October
Uber Eats saw 500 AI‑initiated orders out of 320 million total trips/orders
CEO Dara Khosrowshahi remains optimistic about future AI agent traction
AI agents currently offer little time savings compared to Uber’s fast app booking

posts.title: Canva lays off over 1,200 people amid slowing growth | TechCrunch
posts.author: Ivan Mehta
posts.summary: Canva announced a 22% workforce reduction, cutting 1,271 employees, as it confronts a slowdown in growth after a decade of expansion. CEO Melanie Perkins explained that the company must reorganize, merge product, growth, and platform teams, and adopt a hybrid work model to streamline communication and broaden employee responsibilities. The layoffs also prompted Canva to revise its revenue growth forecast from 30% to 20% and saw its valuation drop to roughly $35 billion, reflecting rising AI costs and intensified competition from AI-driven design tools. Despite these challenges, Canva continues to develop its own AI models to lower dependence on third‑party services while navigating a market increasingly dominated by general‑purpose chatbots like ChatGPT and Gemini.
key_points: Canva is cutting 1,271 staff, a 22% reduction, amid slowed growth.
The company is merging product, growth, and platform teams and shifting to hybrid work to reduce friction.
Canva lowered its revenue growth forecast to 20% and valuation to $35 billion due to rising AI costs.
Competition from AI startups and chatbots like ChatGPT and Gemini is intensifying Canva’s market pressure.

posts.title: Ferrari’s controversial Luce EV is sold out for 2027 | TechCrunch
posts.author: Kirsten Korosec
posts.summary: Ferrari’s first electric car, the Luce, designed by former Apple design chief Jony Ive, has sold out for its 2027 production run, with every planned vehicle already allocated to buyers and deliveries slated to begin in the fourth quarter. The 2027 model starts at about $615,000, and while Ferrari has not disclosed exact production numbers, it is expected to produce fewer than 500 units this year and aims for 2,500 units by 2030. Ferrari’s third‑quarter financials showed a 7% rise in revenue to €1.9 billion and a 13% increase in net income to €431 million, prompting the company to lift its full‑year adjusted earnings guidance to at least €3 billion. Customization sales, which account for more than 21% of revenue from cars and spare parts, helped drive the strong profitability and underscore the brand’s focus on personalized luxury.
key_points: The Luce electric car is sold out for its 2027 production run, with all units already allocated to buyers.
Ferrari’s Q3 revenue rose 7% to €1.9 billion and net income up 13% to €431 million, leading to a higher full‑year earnings forecast.
Customization revenue exceeds 21% of total car and spare‑parts revenue, boosting profitability.
Ferrari plans to produce under 500 Luce units in 2027 and targets 2,500 units by 2030, though exact numbers remain undisclosed.

posts.title: Google faces backlash for plan that would turn off Search for schools that restrict AI | TechCrunch
posts.author: Amanda Silberling
posts.summary: Google announced that K‑12 schools using its education suite will lose access to Google Search unless they opt in to its AI tools such as Gemini, sparking immediate backlash from educators, politicians, and antitrust advocates. The company said the change is meant to give schools more control over AI use, but critics argue it coerces schools into adopting Google’s AI and threatens a monopoly over essential search services. Senators Bernie Sanders and Richard Blumenthal, former FTC chair Lina Khan, and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani condemned the move as extortion and anticompetitive. Google has clarified that AI features are off by default and schools can enable Gemini, Gemini Notebook, and Search individually while it develops a “Guided Learning” tool to help students learn rather than simply receive answers.
key_points: Google will block Search for schools that do not opt in to its AI tools, prompting accusations of coercion and antitrust violations.
The move is framed as giving schools more control, but critics see it as leveraging Google’s search monopoly to force AI adoption.
Google has stated AI features are off by default and can be enabled separately, and it is working on a Guided Learning feature to support student learning.

posts.title: Titan OS raises $46 million to expand its smart TV OS internationally | TechCrunch
posts.author: Ivan Mehta
posts.summary: Barcelona-based Titan OS raised $46 million in new equity and debt financing, bringing its total capital to $110 million. The funding, sourced from BlackRock‑managed debt facilities and existing investors Highland Europe and Mangrove Capital Partners, will accelerate the company’s ambition to expand its TV OS into new markets and deepen partnerships with manufacturers and content providers. With 30 million users and a growing roster that now includes Philips, Sharp, AOC, Vestel, Skyworth, TiVo and Tubi, Titan OS positions itself as a monetization platform that offers advertisers access to a larger, AI‑enhanced audience. The company plans to invest in AI‑driven content discovery and ad recommendation to reduce search time and attract more sales partners, while opening a London office to focus on advertising.
key_points: Titan OS secured $46 million in new equity and debt, raising total funding to $110 million.
The company now serves 30 million users and has partnered with major brands such as Philips, Sharp, and TiVo.
Funding will support AI‑powered content discovery and ad recommendation to improve user experience and advertiser reach.
Titan OS is expanding globally, opening a London office and targeting additional manufacturers to adopt its OS.

posts.title: Anthropic is working on a system to prove AI models' identity | TechCrunch
posts.author: Russell Brandom
posts.summary: Anthropic has announced FlashProve, an open‑source system that uses cryptographic proofs to verify which AI model produced a given output. The system requires labs to publish a model fingerprint that can be matched to outputs without revealing internal weights, allowing users to confirm that responses come from the claimed model. FlashProve could prevent model swapping, protect commercial interests, and enable third parties to verify claims about model usage. The researchers released a technical spec and code on GitHub, but have no immediate plans to deploy the system.
key_points: FlashProve provides cryptographic proof that an output came from a specific AI model.
Labs publish a fingerprint that does not expose model weights, enabling verification for commercial models.
The system can prevent model swapping and allow third parties to verify claims about model usage.
Anthropic released the specification and code on GitHub but will not deploy it immediately.

posts.title: Ten years later, 'Pokémon Go to the polls' still haunts the internet | TechCrunch
posts.author: Amanda Silberling
posts.summary: During Hillary Clinton’s 2016 campaign, she referenced Pokémon GO in a rally, sparking the meme “Pokémon Go to the polls” that has resurfaced every U.S. election. The meme now serves as a reminder of how early‑internet culture—when Facebook, Twitter, and Tumblr dominated—has been replaced by AI‑generated content and a fragmented digital landscape. 2016 is nostalgically remembered as a “good year” for many, with Spotify playlists and Instagram posts spiking as people shared throwback content. The meme’s persistence across the political spectrum shows how humor and a call to vote can coexist in a cynical, algorithm‑driven era.
key_points: The meme “Pokémon Go to the polls” originated from Hillary Clinton’s 2016 rally and reappears at each election.
It highlights the shift from early‑internet culture to an AI‑driven, fragmented online political landscape.
2016 is nostalgically celebrated as a “good year,” reflected in viral playlists and social media posts.
The meme’s cross‑party appeal underscores a shared, ironic plea to encourage voter turnout.

posts.title: Data centers are turning to old jet engines as the wait for power grows | TechCrunch
posts.author: Aditya Mehta
posts.summary: Some AI data centers are retrofitting retired jet engines to burn natural gas because grid connections and new turbines are taking years to come online. The converted units can be deployed in as little as 24 months, a stark contrast to the seven‑year timeline for a 100‑MW grid hookup in Northern Virginia. Companies such as xAI, OpenAI, and the Denver‑based Crusoe have already installed or ordered dozens of these engines, while others have abandoned larger turbine deals in favor of the quicker solution. Although the jet‑engine turbines are less efficient and more polluting than purpose‑built gas plants, they offer a short‑term fix that may become less attractive as efficiency and environmental concerns rise.
key_points: Retired jet engines are being converted to natural‑gas turbines to power AI data centers quickly.
Deployment can be achieved in about 24 months, compared to 7 years for conventional grid connections.
Major players like xAI, OpenAI, and Crusoe are already using or ordering these units.
The technology is less efficient and more polluting, making it a temporary solution.

posts.title: Netflix's new AI Discover tab helps you find something to watch based on your mood | TechCrunch
posts.author: Aisha Malik
posts.summary: Netflix has launched an AI Discover tab that lets users find shows based on their current mood, offering curated themes such as "scare me" and "quick watches". The feature uses a new AI layer that learns from real‑time user input and lets viewers tune recommendations by adding or excluding titles. Netflix calls the tab a "test kitchen" where it experiments with discovery options and collects feedback before integrating them into the main experience. The rollout began in the U.S. for English‑TV users and will expand to other markets in the coming weeks.
key_points: Netflix introduces an AI Discover tab for mood‑based recommendations
Curated themes and a Tune Your Recommendations button let users refine suggestions
The tab serves as a test kitchen for new discovery features and gathers user feedback
Initial rollout is in the U.S. for English‑TV users with plans for broader expansion

posts.title: CrowdStrike to shell out nearly $500M for 2 AI security startups as the market for securing agents takes off | TechCrunch
posts.author: Ram Iyer
posts.summary: CrowdStrike announced acquisitions of Fiddler AI and Dreadnode for roughly $400 million and $95 million respectively, expanding its Falcon platform to monitor and test AI agents and models. The deals come as enterprises deploy AI agents at scale, creating new security gaps that traditional tools struggle to cover. Fiddler AI will become Falcon Observe, providing observability of agent behavior, while Dreadnode will feed automated security testing into Falcon Guardian. These moves position CrowdStrike to capture a growing market for AI‑centric security solutions.
key_points: CrowdStrike is paying about $400 million for Fiddler AI and $95 million for Dreadnode to broaden its AI security offerings
Fiddler AI will be integrated as Falcon Observe to monitor AI agent behavior, while Dreadnode will enhance Falcon Guardian with automated testing
The acquisitions address the security challenges posed by widespread AI agent deployment across enterprises
The moves aim to capture a rapidly expanding market for AI‑centric security solutions

posts.title: Exclusive: Rivian spinout Also was working on an e-moto project in Kenya — until it walked away
posts.author: Sean O'Kane
posts.summary: Also, a micromobility startup spun out of Rivian in 2025, quietly abandoned an electric two‑wheeler pilot in Kenya after receiving a Shell Foundation grant, choosing instead to concentrate on its consumer e‑bike TM‑B and autonomous vehicle work. The Kenya project, aimed at creating a locally integrated electric motorcycle for African riders, was halted after early‑stage work and a shift in priorities toward DoorDash‑partnered small autonomous vehicles. Supply‑chain disruptions delayed the launch of Also’s flagship TM‑B, causing customer frustration and communication gaps, but the company has begun shipping units in early October and is improving its outreach. The move underscores Also’s focus on scalable, cost‑optimized vehicles and its broader ambitions to sell commercial cargo bikes to firms like Amazon.
key_points: Also withdrew from a Shell Foundation‑funded Kenya electric‑motorcycle pilot to focus on its e‑bike TM‑B and autonomous vehicle roadmap.
Supply‑chain challenges delayed the TM‑B launch, leading to customer frustration and a communication overhaul.
The company is partnering with DoorDash on small autonomous vehicles and plans commercial cargo bikes for Amazon.
The Kenya project aimed to test modular batteries and distributed charging for African riders but was abandoned after early‑stage work.

posts.title: Google will let schools disable its AI tools, but not without sacrificing Search | TechCrunch
posts.author: Aisha Malik
posts.summary: Google announced it will disable its AI tools for K‑12 students next year unless school administrators explicitly turn them on, a move that also removes Google Search from schools that opt out because AI features are now embedded in the search engine. The change follows consultations with educators, researchers and policymakers and reflects Google’s intent to give school leaders control over AI use while maintaining its dominant suite of classroom apps. Schools that want to keep access to Search will have to accept its AI features, creating a trade‑off between search functionality and AI restrictions. Google also unveiled Guided Learning, an AI tutor designed to help students build deeper understanding rather than just provide answers.
key_points: Google will disable AI tools for K‑12 unless administrators enable them
Disabling AI also disables Google Search for those schools
Schools face a trade‑off between search access and AI restrictions
Google launched Guided Learning, an AI tutor for deeper learning

posts.title: Ted Schlein's Ballistic Ventures seeks $490M for new funds amid AI-driven cybersecurity boom | TechCrunch
posts.author: Jagmeet Singh
posts.summary: Ballistic Ventures, a San Francisco‑based cybersecurity VC founded in 2021 by former Kleiner Perkins partner Ted Schlein, has filed to raise $490 million across two new vehicles: a $360 million third flagship fund and a $130 million separate Fund B. The move comes amid a surge in AI‑driven cyber threats, which has pushed U.S. cybersecurity startups to raise $11.5 billion in 2025, the highest total since 2022, and made AI‑enabled companies account for 72% of deals through May. Ballistic’s founding team—comprising Schlein, former AT&T Cybersecurity president Barmak Meftah, and Roger Thornton—has backed notable firms such as Talon Cyber Security, Pangea, and others, positioning the firm to capitalize on the growing intersection of AI and cybersecurity.
key_points: Ballistic Ventures is raising $490M across a $360M flagship fund and a $130M Fund B to support AI‑driven cybersecurity startups
AI‑enabled cyber threats have driven 72% of U.S. cybersecurity deals through May, contributing to a record $11.5B raised in 2025
The firm’s founders include Ted Schlein, Barmak Meftah, and Roger Thornton, and it has backed companies like Talon Cyber Security and Pangea
Ballistic’s fundraising reflects the broader trend of venture capital focusing on cybersecurity amid rising AI‑powered attack capabilities

posts.title: AI inference startup Fal doubles its valuation to $16B as demand surges | TechCrunch
posts.author: Marina Temkin
posts.summary: Fal, a San Francisco-based AI inference startup, has doubled its valuation to $16 billion after closing a $1.3 billion Series F round led by Bessemer Venture Partners and joined by Nvidia, Sound Ventures, and T. Rowe Price. The company announced that the combined Series E and Series F rounds raised $1.65 billion, with Sequoia having led the earlier round. Fal’s annualized revenue exceeded $800 million earlier this year, underscoring the rapid growth of demand for inference services that run pre‑trained AI models. The valuation jump highlights the high expectations for inference providers, even as many face thin margins due to costly compute resources.
key_points: Fal’s valuation doubled to $16 billion after a $1.3 billion Series F round led by Bessemer Venture Partners.
The combined Series E and Series F rounds raised $1.65 billion, with Nvidia and Bessemer as key investors.
Fal’s annualized revenue surpassed $800 million, reflecting the surge in demand for AI inference services.

posts.title: Reddit tests ads in search results as traffic declines and growth concerns mount | TechCrunch
posts.author: Sarah Perez
posts.summary: Reddit is testing ad placements in its search results pages as it faces a decline in search traffic and a weaker-than‑expected revenue outlook. The company announced the trial on Tuesday, offering contextual ads that match users’ search queries, such as espresso‑related products for a search on "espresso station." The move comes after the platform beat earnings estimates but issued fourth‑quarter guidance below Wall Street expectations, citing reduced traffic from Google’s AI‑powered search. Reddit also plans a gradual shift to a logged‑in experience to protect against AI scraping and to provide advertisers with richer user data, potentially boosting ad revenue.
key_points: Reddit is launching contextual search‑result ads to offset declining search traffic and strengthen monetization.
Q3 revenue beat expectations but fourth‑quarter guidance fell short, largely due to AI‑driven traffic loss from Google.
The company is moving toward a logged‑in user model to enhance ad targeting and guard against AI scraping.
The new ad test and login shift aim to increase revenue from existing users amid flat or falling daily active user numbers.

posts.title: Anthropic is still grappling with the economics of compute | TechCrunch
posts.author: Russell Brandom
posts.summary: Anthropic disclosed that its compute costs now consume 58% of revenue, up from 48% a quarter earlier, even as revenue rose to $17 billion. The company’s operating loss grew because a $10 billion compute bill—half of it under short‑term contracts—outpaced revenue gains. Anthropic is still courting high‑rate neoclouds such as SpaceX, Nscale, Akamai and Volta while working on its own “Anthropic Direct” compute base, but the rapid demand growth keeps costs high. The worsening margins highlight the vulnerability of AI labs to infrastructure pricing as they near IPO and seek investor confidence.
key_points: Compute costs rose to 58% of revenue, up from 48% a quarter earlier
Anthropic’s $10 billion compute bill included $5 billion under short‑term commitments
Revenue grew to $17 billion but operating loss widened
The firm relies on high‑rate neoclouds and is developing its own compute base under Anthropic Direct

posts.title: Hiding inside Palantir's skyrocketing quarter is a foreboding signal | TechCrunch
posts.author: Julie Bort
posts.summary: Palantir reported a record third‑quarter revenue of $2.31 billion, up 96% year‑over‑year and 20% from the prior quarter, beating analysts’ $2.18 billion forecast and marking the first time the company topped $2 billion in a single quarter. The company also posted adjusted earnings per share of 44 cents versus the expected 41 cents, and raised its full‑year revenue guidance to more than $3.559 billion, a 143% growth rate. However, enterprise sales showed signs of slowing, with total contract value falling from $2.13 billion in the previous quarter to $1.46 billion, and CEO Alex Karp warned that many corporate customers are signing short‑term trials that may be cancelled. Despite the upbeat numbers, the mixed signals about enterprise adoption and contract longevity raise questions about Palantir’s long‑term growth trajectory.
key_points: Palantir’s Q3 revenue hit $2.31 billion, the first time it exceeded $2 billion in a quarter and beat consensus expectations
U.S. commercial revenue ($984 million) surpassed U.S. government revenue ($953 million) for the first time, yet total contract value fell from $2.13 billion to $1.46 billion, indicating slowing sales
CEO Alex Karp highlighted that many enterprise customers are engaging in short‑term trials that can be cancelled, signaling a potential churn risk
The company raised its full‑year commercial revenue guidance to over $3.559 billion, projecting at least 143% growth

posts.title: Orbital Matter 3D-printed the first rigid beam in the vacuum of space | TechCrunch
posts.author: Tim Fernholz
posts.summary: Orbital Matter’s Replicator 2 satellite, launched on a SpaceX rideshare, 3D‑printed a half‑meter rigid beam in orbit, marking the first time a free‑flying spacecraft has built a structural element in space. The demonstration shows that in‑orbit manufacturing can create large solar arrays and other components, potentially easing the power and heat‑dissipation challenges of future orbital data centers. The company plans a 2028 mission that will test a larger printer capable of producing a 5 kW solar array, with a goal of 100+ kW arrays by 2030. Orbital Matter is partnering with ESA, Thales Alenia, NASA and Redwire to integrate its printer‑assisted deployment system into commercial satellites.
key_points: First rigid beam (0.5 m) 3D‑printed in orbit by Orbital Matter’s Replicator 2
In‑orbit manufacturing can enable large solar arrays and structures, easing power and heat challenges
Planned 2028 mission aims for a 5 kW solar array, targeting 100+ kW arrays by 2030
Collaborations with ESA, Thales Alenia, NASA and Redwire to integrate the technology into commercial satellites

posts.title: Researchers warned of North Korean hacking tactics years before record $6.3B Binance heist | TechCrunch
posts.author: Zack Whittaker
posts.summary: Binance confirmed that a North Korean hacking group used a months‑long social engineering campaign to trick a wallet‑team engineer into downloading malicious code, which then allowed the attackers to compromise multiple systems and steal a record $6.3 billion in cryptocurrency. The attackers posed as recruiters offering a job, sending a fake coding assignment that contained malware, and later leveraged credentials stolen from a second engineer who had previously downloaded a tampered app. The incident prompted Binance to suspend withdrawals, review its security posture, and bring in external cybersecurity experts. The heist underscores the persistent threat posed by state‑sponsored actors targeting the crypto industry through elaborate social‑engineering tactics.
key_points: North Korean hackers used fake recruiter personas to infect Binance’s systems via a malicious coding assignment
The attack exploited multiple compromised engineer accounts, enabling access to a tool that controls billions of dollars in crypto
Binance has suspended withdrawals, upgraded security measures, and engaged external experts after the theft

posts.title: Google takes Dreambeans to India in bid to bring AI-generated personal stories to the masses | TechCrunch
posts.author: Jagmeet Singh
posts.summary: Google has expanded its experimental AI app Dreambeans to India, making it the first market outside the U.S. The launch includes support for 13 local languages, such as Hindi, Punjabi, Tamil, Telugu, Bengali, and English, and leverages data from Google services like Calendar, Gemini, Gmail, Photos, Search, and YouTube to generate personalized illustrated and animated stories. While the app has seen modest downloads in the U.S., its entry into India aims to tap a large user base that frequently uses Google’s ecosystem, though language mixing and privacy concerns may limit adoption. Google says users can control which services feed the app, delete data, and set content filters to mitigate sensitive or unwanted stories.
key_points: Dreambeans is now available in India with 13 language options, targeting a market that heavily uses Google services.
The app automatically creates personalized visual stories from users’ Google data without prompts, adding animated elements via Veo.
Privacy controls let users choose connected services, delete data, and filter content, but the reliance on personal data raises concerns.
Downloads in the U.S. peaked in September but fell sharply in October, indicating early adoption challenges.

posts.title: Anthropic warns that it's very close to RSI capability, aka self-building AI | TechCrunch
posts.author: Julie Bort
posts.summary: Anthropic’s revised S‑1/A filing reveals the company believes it is on the brink of creating a model capable of recursive self‑improvement (RSI), a milestone that could accelerate AI progress dramatically. The lab acknowledges that using AI to build more capable AI poses significant safety risks and has outlined a Responsible Scaling Policy to monitor and mitigate those risks. While no current model has crossed the RSI threshold, Anthropic stresses that human oversight will remain integral to frontier model development. The announcement underscores the dual promise and peril of RSI and signals the need for proactive governance as AI capabilities surge.
key_points: Anthropic says it is close to achieving recursive self‑improvement, a milestone that could accelerate AI progress dramatically.
The company has a Responsible Scaling Policy to monitor and mitigate safety risks associated with rapid AI development.
No current model has yet crossed the RSI threshold, and human oversight will continue to guide frontier model creation.
Rapid progress could outpace safety measures, prompting the need for proactive governance and regulation.

posts.title: New York City's Mamdani criticizes Madison Square Garden owner over surveillance tech | TechCrunch
posts.author: Zack Whittaker
posts.summary: Mayor Zohran Mamdani criticized Madison Square Garden owner James Dolan for using surveillance and facial‑recognition technology, arguing it violates privacy and should be banned. He praised local legislation introduced by Councilmember Shahana Hanif that would prohibit biometric data collection in public spaces. Wired reports reveal MSG maintains a database that flags visitors, including celebrities, as LGBTQIA and has used facial‑recognition to identify a lawyer who sued the company, leading to a lawsuit against Wired. MSG denies the claims and says it is pursuing legal remedies, while New York City has required businesses to disclose biometric data collection since 2021.
key_points: NYC Mayor Mamdani calls for banning MSG's facial‑recognition surveillance and supports new biometric‑data legislation.
Wired exposed MSG’s database that labels visitors as LGBTQIA and used facial‑recognition to identify a lawyer, prompting a lawsuit.
MSG denies the allegations and is pursuing legal action against Wired.

posts.title: Apple restricts dating apps and AI companions to users 18 and up | TechCrunch
posts.author: Sarah Perez
posts.summary: Apple is tightening its App Store policies to restrict dating and AI companion apps to users 18 and older, requiring developers to add new content descriptors and an 18+ rating by November 16. The rule also covers apps that share real‑world locations and aims to protect minors through age assurance technology and enhanced parental controls. Popular AI companion services such as Character.AI, Replika, and xAI could be affected, as they often target younger audiences and offer romantic or sexual content. This move follows Apple’s broader effort to improve child safety across its ecosystem.

The policy also targets AI companion apps and location‑sharing features

posts.title: Tomorrow: Founder Summit takes over Boston and when pass rates increase | TechCrunch

posts.title: Yvonne Bajela is bringing $17M in fresh capital to Europe's startup scene | TechCrunch
posts.author: Dominic-Madori Davis
posts.summary: Yvonne Bajela launched Evertrue Capital, closing an oversubscribed $17M Fund I focused on early‑stage AI and fintech in the UK and Europe. She brings a decade of VC experience from LocalGlobe and Impact X, having backed companies like Wise and Mooves. The fund plans to invest about £350k per deal and target 20 companies over three years, with 80% of LPs UK‑based. Bajela cites the AI boom and a democratized building landscape as reasons for timing, while noting fundraising remains tough even in a supportive UK market.

posts.title: Apple Watch's AI features for rewinding and recapping conversations begin beta testing | TechCrunch
posts.author: Sarah Perez
posts.summary: Apple has begun beta testing its new Audio Intelligence suite on the Apple Watch, launching the features in the iOS 27.3 update for developers. The four opt‑in tools include sound and song recognition, Live Rewind—which lets users double‑press the crown to view a 15‑second text snippet of the last conversation—and Siri Recaps, which summarizes conversations into bullet points without recording raw audio. Apple emphasizes privacy by processing audio on the watch’s S11 chip, encrypting data in a secure enclave, and deleting summaries from its Private Cloud Compute immediately after use. The beta will later expand to a public test before the features become available to all users.

Siri Recaps generates concise, speaker‑agnostic summaries that can be exported to Notes or Journal and are deleted after seven days if not saved
Audio is processed on the watch and iPhone in a secure enclave, with no raw audio stored or sent to Apple

posts.title: Trajectory raises $45M to make AI model training accessible to nontechnical experts | TechCrunch
posts.author: Marina Temkin
posts.summary: Trajectory, a Stanford‑born startup, has raised $45 million in a Series A led by Sequoia and backed by Nvidia, Bessemer Venture Partners, and Bain Capital Ventures, valuing the 18‑person company at $300 million. The firm offers a continual‑learning platform that lets businesses fine‑tune open‑source AI models with real‑world feedback, enabling lawyers, doctors, and other specialists to improve models without hiring costly research teams. By automating post‑training, Trajectory aims to make specialized AI deployment faster, cheaper, and accessible to nontechnical users. The platform is already used by companies such as Harvey, Rogo, Decagon, Mercor, and Nvidia, and it competes with other post‑training startups like Thinking Machines Lab, Applied Compute, and Prime Intellect.
